identification.title: God Will Make a Way
identification.notes: Written by Don Moen, then president of Integrity Music, after the death of a child of his sister-in-law Susan and her husband Craig Phelps in a van accident. Crosswalk's song story says he sketched it on a legal pad on the flight to the funeral after reading Isaiah 43, sang it to the family, then at a church in Alabama and an Integrity staff devotional, and F. G. Baldwin suggested recording it on the Integrity project Eternal God. Dates conflict among sources I saw: one search result dated the flight to 1987, others give later releases; the 1990 year of the live Eternal God recording is taken from the reading note and was not confirmed by a fetched page. Publisher and CCLI number were not found on any page loaded; Integrity Music is the label. The list's guess of Don Moen is right for the writer and recording. Reviewed as the song, not any one recording.

claims.structuralNotes: One long chorus of eight lines sung about four times, with a short bridge-like section between repeats and a tag at the end. The whole is in the third person about God, speaking to the congregation and the singer rather than addressing him. The chorus says God provides a path where none can be seen, works unseen, will guide, hold the singer close and give strength for each day. The bridge says he leads through wilderness and desert with rivers, that heaven and earth pass but his word stands, and that he does something new. The acts of God named are providential guidance and provision. Christ, the cross, the resurrection and the return are not reached, and the Spirit is not named. The voice is personal trust and expectation.

strengths.title: Trust grounded in God's word
strengths.explanation: The song's confidence rests on a promise taken from Scripture, that God opens a way in the wilderness, and not on the singer's resolve. The comfort is anchored in who God is and what he has said.
strengths.scriptureRationale: A way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert - the promise the song is built on.

strengths.title: The word that outlasts heaven and earth
strengths.explanation: The bridge sets God's word above all that passes, which gives the promise of guidance a firm base.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The grass withers but the word of our God stands forever.

strengths.title: Guidance and daily strength
strengths.explanation: The chorus asks the singer to expect God's guiding and sustaining care, one day at a time, a theme Scripture holds out to believers.
strengths.scriptureRationale: God holding the believer's hand and guiding him with counsel.

theological.assessment: Nothing to correct. The promise is general guidance and provision, not a guarantee of specific outcomes, and Old Testament promise language applied personally is a common and acceptable use. Crosswalk's song story presents it as trust in God's unseen work in suffering. What the song does not reach is the gospel: Christ, the cross and the resurrection are absent, so it comforts without saying why God can be trusted. No independent assessment of its teaching was found.

strengths.title: Very easy to learn
strengths.explanation: A single chorus repeated and one short bridge make the song learnable in one hearing.

strengths.title: Born in grief, suited to hard seasons
strengths.explanation: It was written for a family after a child's death, and the origin shows in a song fit for funerals, hospital visits and times of loss.

communal.vocalRangeNote: No published key was confirmed for this review. Test the chorus with the room before choosing a key.

range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: The long chorus returns about four times with only a short bridge between, so repetition carries much of the song, though the chorus itself holds substantial content.
communal.assessment: Congregational and easy to sing, with a chorus long enough to say something. The heavy return of one chorus is the main practical point. It comforts the singer in the first person but without the gospel.

strengths.title: The promise is plain
strengths.explanation: The song says plainly what it trusts God to do: guide, provide and strengthen.

clarity.assessment: Clear in its claims. Its wilderness and desert imagery is Isaiah's, and the promise is general rather than specific.

synthesis.summary: A song of trust built on Isaiah 43:19: God makes a way where none is seen, guides, holds the singer close and gives strength daily, and his word outlasts heaven and earth. Written by Moen after a child's death in his wife's family. Christ and the cross are not reached, and the voice is personal confidence more than creed. Nothing in it is false. No independent assessment of its teaching was found.
